utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are here. I'm looking at the Defence teams. I notice the absence of Mr. Bourgon only and Mr. Krgovic, Mr. Krgovic. The Prosecution, we have Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Nicholls and Mr. Thayer. All right. Let me start with the leftovers from yesterday's sitting. Mr. Haynes and Mr. McCloskey, we had a short discussion yesterday following the examination of your list of documents, Mr. Haynes rather than Mr. McCloskey, with the Butler testimony, and at that time Mr. McCloskey raised some issues in relation to two documents; that is, witness statement of Sabic, Vejiz, 7D234 and that of Milan Maric, 7D272, and the agreement was that you would have a tete-a-tete discussion following the sitting and inform the Trial Chamber of the outcome of your discussions. What's the outcome, please? Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We have created two new exhibits. I believe they will be, when they're uploaded into e-court as they presently are, being 7D725 and 7D726. They are respectively the portions of those interviews or witness statements which were either read to or read by Mr. Butler during the course of his cross-examination, and I sent them by e-mail to Mr. McCloskey. He's briefly had the opportunity to look at them. I hope that it will be agreed that 7D725 and 726 will be tendered into evidence. I've been reminded that I should point out to you that -- so that they can be identified, those exhibits also include the first page of the interview or witness statement so you know who it is. But other than that, I think one is two pages and one is one page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine, Mr. President. We're fine with that, the way he's defined it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So the bottom line is you are no longer requesting putting into evidence 7D234 and 272, and you're replacing those by 7D725 and 726, to which there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So 7D725 and 7D726, even though it may well be the case that they are not yet in e-court, are being admitted. All right. Then yesterday, when we were discussing the Nikolic Defence team list of documents, you, Mr. McCloskey, raised an objection in relation to 3D274, which is an e-mail dated 13th January 2008, sent by Ms. Stewart, on your behalf, to all the Defence teams, which I don't need to read. Following the submissions, you agreed, at the invitation of the Trial Chamber, that you would meet and try to come to a conclusion or to an agreement. Have you reached an agreement, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I do believe we have reached an agreement. Mr. McCloskey and I exchanged several messages in that regard. The witness was examined on the matters contained in Mr. McCloskey's e-mail, and it is true that the document was not shown to the witness. However, Mr. McCloskey and I agreed that there is no longer an objection, and since the witness was asked some questions in relation to this, Mr. McCloskey would no longer oppose the admission of this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Mr. McCloskey, do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, mostly. This e-mail was never made reference to. Some of the subject matter in it was, and to that degree I have no objection to the e-mail itself coming in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. One question to both of you. This e-mail, in the first page at the top, there is an indication of all the e-mail addresses of everyone. That includes Ms. Stewart's and that also includes yours and Mr. Mitchell's. Do you wish to retain it as it is or would you like at least to redact or -- redact that part which is not necessary for the purposes that you intend the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could redact all those addresses, that's a very good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I don't think they are of any use to anybody, and if it's going to be public, I don't think this should be public domain.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I agree too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So, Mr. Registrar, you'll look after this. Let me show you what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we are redacting the entire top part of the document, including who sent it and who were the addressees. I think from the rest of the debate, it should be clear what we're talking about. All right. That disposes of this second. So 3D274, with the understanding that a part thereof that's being redacted, it's being admitted. Yes. Something which this was the easiest of all the issues we left pending yesterday, I'm sure you have reached an agreement, a stipulation, we're talking of P45, alias P1059. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm glad to say we have, Your Honour, although there is one added complication which Mr. McCloskey will tell you about in a moment. So far as P1059 is concerned, we are prepared to stipulate that this document was handed to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 18th of February of the year 2000 by Nenad Petrusic, and I've discussed that not just with Mr. McCloskey but also with Madame Fauveau, of course. So far as P45 is concerned, we are prepared to stipulate that that document was handed to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 2nd of June of the year 2003 by Dragan Obrenovic. So that's as far as we are prepared to go. As I say, there is now an added complication which my learned friend will no doubt address you about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for your practical approach, Mr. Josse, which is typical of you and which we appreciate. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Regarding the first one, 1059, that's correct, and the language that Mr. Josse used is basically right out of our -- what we call our "myth form," indicating how it was received. It's actually by Mr. Mark Harmon from Mr. Petrusic. The next one, number 45, is right out of the form. Actually, it was received by counsel for Obrenovic, Dusan Slijepcevic. I have the actual forms, if that's easier. I don't really -- It doesn't matter to me, if it's just part of the oral record and the form. And the interesting addition to that is I'd asked, oh, for one last complete review of our collections to see if it might -- this document might be found in another form, and it was found -- an original copy of it was found in the Drina Corps collection. And I have a 65 ter number just given to me by Ms. Stewart, 3205. It came under the name of Ulan Gazero [phoen], so we had to get a little trickier in our search to find that; but it's clearly the identical document that came from the Drina Corps. It's not loaded in e-court. I would like to offer that into evidence, as it appears to be contested. I guess it's M. Ulan Gazero, to be more exact, is how it came out, but it's clearly the identical document from the Drina Corps collection, so that you now see this document coming from Mr. Obrenovic and coming from the Krstic Defence team, and now the Drina Corps collection. And this document is also -- the number of it -- the VRS number 34-1629, is referred to in other documents in this case, and I won't go into that, but that is roughly the history of this. And I think you having the complete history is a good idea in this particular situation, but I don't feel the Prosecution needs to go any further into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it identical to the other two?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. In my -- it's clearly the same document. I haven't looked at it to see if there's -- you know, teleprinters sometimes do different things, but it's clearly the same number document, the wording is the same, and -- sorry, it was 3250 is the -- we've reversed some numbers ourselves. So the Drina Corps 65 ter number is 3250, and from our brief review of it, it's clearly the same document. We have not done an analysis to see what other, maybe, mistypes in the teleprinter or other things are on it, but it's clearly the same document. And it's an original, as I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's the same, I think I know the answer, but if it's the same, why do you want to make it three if you've already got two of the same document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, because there appears to be a challenge to the authenticity, and -- you know the history of Mr. Obrenovic's retrieval of the document. The history of the document that came from the Krstic Defence came from the RS, which is -- is my understanding is a whole other history. And so I think the third time is the charm on this one. It came from the Drina Corps, so I think that those three things should establish its authenticity beyond any possible reasonable doubt, which of course is my objective here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would not like to suggest that the authenticity of the document is not in dispute. A double negative, I'm sorry, but I'm sure the Court gets the gist of what I'm saying. There again, in effect, this document is being offered up today from the Bar table, and I also appreciate that it might be said, with some justification, that the Defence have brought this upon themselves because of the stance that we have taken in relation to 45 and 1059. That I also recognise. The Chamber may or may not be aware that there is to be an application by the Prosecution to adduce a not-inconsiderable number of other documents, in effect, through the Bar table. Mr. McCloskey has explained a technical reason, which I accept, as to why this document is not in that motion, largely because it's late discovery. He and I only discussed the matter at about noon today. What I would invite the Chamber to do is to allow the Defence to lump this document in with the Bar table motion and to respond at that particular juncture. In other words, we'd ask for some time before responding to the submission. So I know it further complicates matters, but I rather think that matters are going to have to be put off in relation to this Prosecution motion. I don't want to jump the gun here, and I certainly don't want to do the Prosecution's work for them in relation to that particular motion or application, but perhaps this document could join that list as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Let me make myself clear, my mind clear on this. And if my colleagues don't agree, then obviously not. As I see it, we raised the issue of MFI'd documents because we're approaching the Rule 98 bis decision -- proceedings. There are already two of these documents, identical, identical twins, and I understand that the differences are, I think in the English translation they are off, rather than the original text; and the question of provenance that hung over our heads yesterday has now been removed. The question of authenticity, as such, can remain unprejudiced, taking up what you have suggested, in; in other words, because the three of them will go in the same basket. However, our position is that for the time being, we agree with your suggestion that rather than deciding on 3250 now, we lump it with -- we group it with the other documents that we are waiting to hear from Mr. McCloskey about. But what is your position as regards 45 and 1059, because I think you need to have that crystallized for the purpose of Rule 98 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I dealt with that, Your Honour. When I stood up, I asked what the stipulation was. That was the stipulation we made so far as 45 and 1059 is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I can also give the Court this cast iron guarantee that 3250 will not make a jot of difference to the 98 bis submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I think as well, but we won't deprive you the opportunity of making submissions. So 45 and 1059 will come in. The other one will stay in limbo together with the others until we dispose of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Aerial images, and specifically we're dealing with MFI'd documents P2103 and P1516. If there are others, they will be put in the same baskets. If there are others, the identification of we are not aware of at the present, they will have the same treatment. We have, in the time we had, carefully considered your submissions relating to the aerial images until now MFI'd with the numbers I mentioned before, 2103 and 1516, and we have done so together with the consultation of the relevant transcripts of past sittings, when we dealt with the issues of -- various issues relating to aerial images, aerial imagery. Our decision is that the reasons adduced by you, Mr. Ostojic, particularly yesterday, for not admitting these documents go to weight rather than the criteria necessary for admission. The Trial Chamber is satisfied that sufficient evidence on the relevance and the probative value of these aerial images has been adduced by the Prosecution. Therefore, all aerial images introduced are admitted without prejudice, of course, to the weight that should or should not be given to them at the end of this case. That disposes of aerial images. Skorpion video.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. We have received an agreement on that. We were talking about it a lot yesterday, and I have a written stipulation I can pass out. It's been passed out to my friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, I have it here. This is -- I've got it here, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. I mean, I thought I was looking at a record stipulation, which would have gone in the "Guinness Book of Records."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thank my friends, because I've been talking with many of them this week and yesterday to resolve the language of this stipulation. This has not been loaded up into e-court yet, but it means that we will not be able to call the witness. I believe he was PW-103. We will not be calling --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was the whole purpose of --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. So if I can just say we've provisionally assigned the numbers 3248 to this stipulation, which is not in e-court yet, but it will be. As I say, we were working it out yesterday afternoon and throughout the court sitting yesterday. The actual video which was played on November 3rd of 2006 would be 3249, and the transcript would have the same number. While I'm on my feet, when we're done with this, I have a few more short stipulations I could run through at this time or later, however the Chamber pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Do I have a confirmation of this from the various Defence teams? If anyone does not agree that this stipulation has been reached or does not agree as to the contents of this stipulation, please stand up. None. So this is your stipulation. I think the document itself needs to be given a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. That would be 3248, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I understood you --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the next number, 3249, would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. This is 3248, and the video will be 3249. Okay. So that disposes of the Skorpion video matter. Yes. You may proceed on the other stipulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Again, I thank my friends. We've reached an agreement, so we will not need to call back Alistair Graham, and I'll pass that to you now. We've got a book that's been passed out to the Defence. It's the identical book that was passed out last week, I think, if I could hand those to Your Honours. That's just for the Chamber, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. We need one more for Judge Kwon here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I think the stipulation which is written on page 1, the first stipulation of this exhibit, makes it quite self-explanatory. It concerns a 12th of March, 2002 interview with Mr. Borovcanin and the discussion of the video DVD which was played at that time. In order to make sense of that interview and follow it, Your Honours need to be able to tell what still image is being discussed in the transcript, and that is the purpose -- the main purpose of this book. The still images are the best that could be copied from the video, and the video is also in evidence. This will be number 3246. And, again, I thank the Borovcanin team, in particular, for being very cooperative on working on this stipulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does anyone of the Defence teams wish to address the Chamber on this stipulation and document? We hear none. So this document, P3246, being stipulations relating to excerpts from the video and interview with Ljubomir Borovcanin, is being admitted and it will form part of the records. Next.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The third, Your Honour, is a very simple stipulation with regard to the evidence of Witness 42, who is not a protected witness, Ahmo Hasic, and it has to do with his description of the school that he was held in Bratunac. And I can either read out this short stipulation into the record, it's a few sentences, or I can pass it out, whichever the Chamber or the Defence prefers. It's been agreed upon by e-mail with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It being e-mail, I would prefer if he reads it out so that we make sure that everyone has received the e-mail and everyone is happy with it. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll read it out, then: "In his testimony, witness Ahmo Hasic (Witness 42) referred to the school where he was detained in Bratunac as the 'Vuk Karadzic' school. In a proofing session on 13 July 2003, the witness circled a building on an aerial photograph of Bratunac, ERN number 0297-8872-0297-8873, and stated that he was 90 per cent sure that this was the building in which he had been detained. The building circled by the witness is the 'old school' in Bratunac, not the 'Vuk Karadzic' school. The old school in Bratunac is located next to the Vuk Karadzic School." That's the end of the stipulation. And the reason for that very briefly, Your Honours, is that this circling of the building was something that had been done in proofing back in 2003. That was disclosed to the Defence, but it didn't come up in his direct or his cross-examination, just this little discrepancy of the description, and we thought it should be before the Chamber just for the whole picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Does any one of the Defence teams wish to address the Trial Chamber? Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Not on this issue, but we do have other -- I have other issues, but not on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll come to you. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The last item on my personal list: At the end of the Witness Zoran Petkovic, I stated that I wanted to put in the transcript of the Studio B video footage documentary. There was no objection, but I said that we were going to, with the cooperation of my friends, revise the transcript to make sure it was correct. We've done that. The revised transcript is in e-court, and the number is P02012, and so now I just formally want to ask that that be admitted. As I say, there was no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from the Defence teams? We hear none, so that addition of the video is being admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just to make you feel more comfortable, Mr. Ostojic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yesterday, my learned friend Madam Nikolic addressed you with respect to the 92 quater motion that was filed, and we were seeking an extension of time. We had agreed to a stipulation with the Prosecution and we need your permission. And I perhaps gave the wrong information. Our stipulation, in fact, was for ten days, and we were going to file the response, and we're hoping to get it jointly, the Defence is meeting on this, by the 22nd of February, which is two days as opposed to the 20th, in light of the scheduling of the 98 bis going into the 20th. So just so that the Court is clear on that, with your permission, we'd like to have leave to have an extension to file that respond on the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Permission granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All right, so ... During the testimony of PW-168, a protected witness, I think it was the Popovic Defence team made use of the statements of three persons. I'm referring to documents 1D383, that being the statement of a certain Nebojsa Jeremic, 1D432, that being the statement of a certain Zoran Jovanovic, and 1D438, that being the statement of a certain Ljubisa Dijolovic [phoen]. These three persons did not testify in these proceedings, in this trial, but their statements, as I said, were used during the cross-examination of the Popovic Defence team. We had MFI'd them at the time and not admitted them, pending our decision as to whether it is appropriate to admit them. We have given this our consideration, and our decision is to admit these three documents under the same terms and for the same reasons as explained in our yesterday's decision re. the Defence motion dealing with the Momir Nikolic statement of facts. So for the same reasons, we -- and under the same terms, we are admitting these three documents. All right. Now, yesterday you will recall that I referred to two pending motions, namely, the one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll return to these two pending motions shortly. Speaking of documents that are still MFI'd and which we would like to regularise, if necessary and if possible, we submitted to you a list, and we are anxious to hear your position. I will start with P2754, which was tendered during the testimony of Witness Milovanovic. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a Main Staff document, not to be confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. My understanding is that this was discussed by Mr. Butler, as the Chamber has already pointed out. It was tendered through General Milovanovic's testimony. I understand that there is no objection from the Miletic Defence team. I note that in particular because this is a document bearing General Miletic's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The problem seemed to be at the time authentication.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In my understanding, there's no challenge to the authenticity of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Does any one of the Defence teams wish to comment? Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. This is just to confirm what my colleague says. Indeed, this document was used with this person, and -- with Mr. Butler, and it was furnished by this person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. So this document is admitted. We come to P2498. Now, this was tendered during the testimony of a protected witness, that was Witness number 49. I won't mention his name. And if we need to mention his name, then we need to go into private session. 2498, this was an UNPROFOR MIMO from David Harland.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and if I may, it may save a little bit of time to discuss it in tandem with the next document as well, P02499.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, which is exactly another document from David Harland.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. The documents, as the e-mail notes, were originally tendered through this witness. What we soon found was that both parties were making liberal use of these reports and updates from Mr. Harland to Mr. Ryan. Subsequently, following the testimony of Mr. Joseph, the Trial Chamber specifically asked that all of the reports be compiled into a packet and tendered. We have done so. Initially at the time, and this was back, I believe, on August 27th of 2007, following Mr. Joseph's testimony, I furnished my friend from the Gvero team an initial copy of the packet. That's been augmented by three other reports, one of which is 2499, and we now have a complete packet. It numbers 18 tabs. There were 16 reports plus two others that were related, all authored by Mr. Harland. I have four sets for Your Honours with the Registrar for distribution. I haven't had much of an opportunity to discuss with my colleagues whether there are any objections. There certainly was none back in August. In fact, the one team that was on the record with respect to the Court's indication that it wished to have these compiled was in full agreement. So we're simply complying with the Court's request, and that would apply to both of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Does any one of the Defence teams wish to comment? Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, since we've been referred to specifically there, and for understandable reasons, we do not object to this course of action. We've known about it for some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And, in fact, I vividly remember I think it was probably yourself expressing a wish to have this compilation because of its eventual utility.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. What is not clear in my mind is whether we are going to retain 2498 and 2499 or whether this is in substitution of either or both of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this a new document?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may have a moment to consult with our technical expert on this. Mr. President, Ms. Stewart advises me that we can put in this entire packet as one document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The index does note the documents that have separate 65 ter numbers, but we can put the entire packet, and that will be 65 ter 3251.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection? No. We hear no objection. One question again, Mr. Thayer -- yes, Mr. Josse, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: After the question, Your Honour. It's on a slightly different but related subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. One question, Mr. Thayer. I notice that in this document, one of the other two documents, 2499, is included, but I don't see 2498, although on the second page I do see 2948. What I want to clarify is to make sure that 2948 has not been mistaken for 2498, and if it's not, whether that means that 2498 needs to be dealt with separately, albeit within the same context of the discussion. Did I make myself clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You did, Mr. President. I'm just cross-checking with the hard copy as I speak. Mr. President, you're correct, that is a -- no, I stand -- let me withdraw that. Tab number 13 should be listed as 2498, and the tab number -- or the 65 ter number tab 15, I believe, is correct, 2948. We were just missing 2498.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So that simplifies the matter. 2498 and 2499 that were tendered separately during the testimony of Witness number 49 are admitted, and similarly we are admitting this new document, 3251, which is a compilation of the various David Harland memoranda. Okay, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Always -- in relation to the same witness, we have got 2503. Now, 2503 was the Podrinje Brigade combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. With respect to this document, I'll take you just through a brief history of it. It was used on redirect with Witness 49. It was objected to at the time the Prosecution tendered it. I think the idea was to MFI it or -- MFI it until another witness came along. That witness was Mr. Joseph, so it was tendered without objection. For some reason, in the interim it got a different 65 ter number, and I think that's why it still remains on our question mark list. It came in under a different 65 ter number, that is, 2671, again on 27 August 2007, through Mr. Joseph, again without objection. So that, I think, is just off the list for that reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Do we need to admit the same document twice? I don't think so. So unless there is some comment, remark, or objection from any one of the Defence teams, I propose to leave it as it is. All right. We have 2671, and that should suffice. Always with the same document, we used 209, which is another Podrinje Brigade combat report. Do you wish to address the Chamber, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. With respect to this document, it was used with Witness 49 on his redirect examination, specifically on the issue of whether the VRS had adhered to various promises that were made in prior agreements. That was an issue pressed on cross-examination. This document was then shown to the witness on the Prosecution theory that it might elicit his comment or elucidation as to whether that, in fact, was the case. At the time, the Trial Chamber wanted to MFI this document, pending use with another witness. This did not become used through another witness. However, I think that the -- that the totality of the evidence that has come in through other witnesses so far, consistent with the Prosecution's theory of the case, warrants the admission of this document, which is probative and relevant of a couple of issues that are very much alive in the case. The first is the nature of this mop-up operation after the transportation of the civilian population from Zepa. It is consistent with the charged events or the named events in the indictment, namely, Nezuk and Snagovo, where what we had was a pattern of systematic, on-the-spot executions of groups of prisoners who were found as this mop-up operation continued. This is perfectly consistent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to what the Prosecutor has said. The document refers to the events in Zepa, but has nothing to do with Snagovo and Zvornik. So I would like the Prosecutor to limit himself to what is said in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Madame Fauveau. We don't have the document in front of us at the moment. I have got notes on it. But what's your position on this objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My position remains, Mr. President, that this document is entirely consistent with what the Prosecution has alleged in connection with the mop-up operation after the Srebrenica operation. And that goes specifically to the reasonableness of fear that the male population of Zepa had at the time that they were faced with the decision of whether to stay or whether to flee. Males of all ages were faced with that. You heard a lot of testimony about what the men in Zepa knew about what had happened in Srebrenica, when they knew about it, and how that information impacted on their decision. What this document shows, and this is not just idle conversation by a VRS officer, this is a daily combat report from a commander, Lieutenant Colonel Rajko Kusic, the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, to the Command of the Drina Corps, describing using ethnically-derogatory terminology, referring to these people who were killed as "balijas," it describes basically executing an unarmed, starving individual in the Zepa area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Prosecutor really wants to keep this argument, he has to keep to the text. There is -- you don't have the word "not armed," so could he read the document as is, because there's a risk of not presenting it properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madame Fauveau. Mr. Thayer, let me put a very blunt question to you. Did you have advanced notice by any of the Defence teams that they were objecting -- they're going to object to the admission of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Beyond the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Today, I mean, or yesterday or today?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Not today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So why surround yourself or build around yourself a battleground?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, precisely because I'm being asked the basis for which this should be admitted, and I'm offering that to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if you had no notice of a pending objection, why go into details, which might trigger an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, in answer to my friend's question, I'd be pleased to read the language that I'm being accused of leaving out, and that is specifically: "The same day, in the vicinity of Luca, an unarmed Ustasha, born in Srebrenica, 24 years old, was liquidated. Before he died, he said that he fell behind the others and he was looking for food."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems also to be a translation problem. This is why I object to this document, because the translation does not correspond to the official text, the B/C/S text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Any further comments, any further objections? Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I come here to argue this procedurally, not substantively. My learned friend's interesting and very emotive address relates to the substance in his assertion that this document is relevant. I suspect that could be said of a great number of documents which are not in evidence. The Prosecution and, indeed, the Defence could create arguments, true or otherwise, as to why they support one or other side's case. I thought that we were here to examine procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Admissibility, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What had happened is what Mr. Thayer has rightly described, which was it wasn't admitted at that point because it was going to be put to another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It hasn't been put to another witness. The Trial Chamber now needs to decide whether it should be admitted. In effect, what he's saying is it again should join the motion, I suppose, in relation to documents coming from the Bar table, because that's really what he's doing, and he's getting a first shot in and making a nice rather emotive speech which understandably is upsetting my learned, Madame Fauveau, who's objection I agree with wholeheartedly, and stirring up a hornets' nest, when it's purely a procedural issue in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is, Mr. Josse, I don't quite read you, when you say it could go with the rest, because it was used with one witness, and it was MFI'd precisely because there was a suggestion at the time, an objection at the time, that that particular witness knew nothing about the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The difference between this one and the previous one is that the previous one was used with another witness, while this one wasn't, but it was still used with this witness. My understanding of what's to come, the pleasures yet to come, is that they have not been used with any witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right. To encapsulate, in our submission, that is, on behalf of General Gvero, the submission is that it was MFI'd at the time on the basis that it had not been proved sufficiently relevant to be admitted at that juncture, that it would be shown to a subsequent witness, and at that juncture might be admitted into evidence. Procedurally, that hasn't happened. In our submission, it shouldn't be admitted. My objection is as limited as that, technical I accept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My information is because that day I was sick eventually and I went home, and that's where the matter ended. There were two objections at the time. One was that this came on you as a surprise and you were not prepared for cross-examining the witness on it, and, do you remember, this was used on redirect and you had no advanced notice of it, and, second, that the witness knew nothing about this document and they should be used with the subsequent witness. That's what I have on record.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right. My objection was at 9888 of the transcript, and again speaking for our team, if the Trial Chamber wanted to decide the issue based on the arguments at that juncture, then we have no difficulty. But we do have a great deal of difficulty the way Mr. Thayer is approaching the matter today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Just shortly, Your Honour, the Beara Defence team would join with Mr. Josse and point out that there's also a difficulty, we believe, in the representations made at the time by the Prosecutor, that, "We will put it to another witness," and they haven't done it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That happens, and we have -- we all have experience of trial -- trial experience, and we know why it happens. So, yes, Mr. Thayer, you have the last word.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think I have anything further to add to what I've already said. I'm just trying to address this issue in the most efficient manner I thought it presented itself to me, which is to move it in now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, Mr. Thayer, Ms. Fauveau, especially the three of you, because you are the ones who contributed to this very useful debate, we agree with most of what you said, Mr. Josse, and also with what you said, Madame Fauveau, that, strictly speaking, the debate should have been limited to what is procedurally required to be proven by the Prosecution for the purpose of admissibility. Now, as we see it, it's as follows: From an examination of the records that we have, and we stand to be corrected if it's not so, but it doesn't appear to us that at any time the provenance or the authenticity of this document was challenged, which would leave us the task of examining whether, for the purpose of admissibility under Rule 89, the Prosecution has proven relevance and probative value. The question that -- it looks from the records that supposedly this document was to be used or the preference shown was that it would be used with some other witness, of course carries its own weight, but that's not for the purpose of admissibility. We don't believe that the fact that a witness has not been used -- a document has not been used with a witness or with more than one witness disqualifies that document from being admitted. We are satisfied that, overall, both the relevance and the probative value of this document has been proven, so it is being admitted with the caveats that I mentioned before. So that disposes of that one. 108. This was used with Witness Trivic, and it's a Drina Corps Command order.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President, and we are in exactly the same situation with this document, I think, as we were with the former one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, this was used on redirect with Colonel Trivic based upon the Prosecution's belief that, on cross-examination, the related issues of whether the Krivaja-95 attack was something that had been planned substantially ahead of time or which was something that was more of an ad hoc plan, and also tied to the treatment and planned treatment of UN personnel by the VRS, there was cross-examination throughout the trial not only of Colonel Trivic but of other witnesses where various documents were shown by my friends to witnesses, highlighting language to the effect of, "We will treat UNPROFOR properly, correctly. They are not our enemy. We will not attack UNPROFOR," and so forth. Now, given the discussion we just had, I'll leave it there. There was no -- there was no further witness who was examined with this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- With this document, which was again used with Colonel Trivic to address those issues of evidence to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any objections? Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, without wanting to go behind the previous decision, perhaps the Defence are on slightly stronger ground here. At page 12135 of the transcript, having heard our objections, Your Honour, the learned Presiding Judge, said this: "So our decision on 65 ter number 108 is since it hasn't really been used with Witness 109, Mirko Trivic, it will not be admitted now. It will remain marked for identification until used with some other witness. If not, it will remain marked for identification and then it will disappear from the list." In our submission, the Court should stand by that decision made at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. With the caveat -- I think you've clarified part of the issue. With the caveat that contrary to the previous one, since it was not used with that witness and it was not used with any other witness, it can come in or the Prosecution can seek to bring it in together with the other documents that they are apparently going to offer from the Bar table, because the same argument you mentioned before applies mutatis mutandis for this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course I accept that, and we all, all seven Defence teams, are going to need to address fully this important development.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely, definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So there is no P0108 for us to consider at the present moment, in conformity or pursuant to our ruling that Mr. Josse has referred to. Do you wish to have it included in the list of documents that you intend to submit, you're free to do so, and then of course without prejudice to what happens after. 345. Now we're coming to Witness Barr, and 345 is a Zvornik Brigade report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This report to the Bijeljina military prosecutor was in fact admitted under a different 65 ter number, and that came in as P00386 through the testimony of Nebojsa Jeremic. I'm afraid I don't have his witness number off the top of my head. It may have been 135 -- 137, I'm informed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, check whether he was a protected witness or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: He was not, Mr. President. He testified in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the date of that admission was 25 April 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree to that, Mr. Ostojic, because you were the one mostly involved in the admissibility of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. So there is no point in discussing it any further, the admittance of -- admission of 345, because it has been admitted under P386. Okay. We also had document 935, P935, which is the IKM logbook.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, that was admitted under a different 65 ter number, P00347, through Mihaljo Galic on 27 April 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And, again, do you stand by that, Mr. Ostojic? I'm asking Mr. Ostojic, it's because he was the one who objected. If anyone else wishes to address the Chamber, please identify yourself. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. So that 3935 we don't need to discuss any further, because that document has already been admitted under P347.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the record, that was Witness 118.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 118, okay, thank you. And finally we come to P1936, which was used with Witness Stanojevic, Dobrisav Stanojevic, and this a compilation of photographs and identification of Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, during the course of the trial there was various references made to this video stills book, which is P01936. We showed various witnesses pages out of this book, sometimes referring to the chapter or page number of this original version. What we subsequently did was create an updated version, in some cases based on trial testimony, in some cases based on other investigation that had been conducted, but it has been updated. Copies of the updated book were distributed sometime, I think, in November to our friends. As I understand it, there is no objection to the new-and-improved version. What we would ask is that we retain both copies in the system, since on occasion there were references throughout the testimony to the old version. So that the record remains intelligible, we'd ask that we retain 1936 and give the new version the number P001937. And the new version, I would respectfully request, be placed under seal, since some of the trial witnesses who were referred to as making these identifications were protected witnesses, and we've used their full names so the various parties don't have to flip back to the witness list. They can just see who it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Their name appears on this new document?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Ms. Stewart, in particular, can you check for us that there isn't already another document which bears the number 1937.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We actually -- we picked that up, Mr. President. That -- that was just a doubling of the same exhibits. So what we're doing is just giving this new document the same number that was there. We'll just change the ERNs that are in the system in e-court. What happened in e-court was for some reason the exhibit was entered twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So now we'll just remove the ERNs, and 1937 will be the new version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection? So no objection to P1936 and no objection to P1937. Instead of one, we now have two, 1936 being the old version, 1937 being the revised one, and P1937 will remain under seal. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have two other pieces of evidence to discuss with the Chamber. One is what we have referred to as the Muslim ID book. This is another collection of still photographs from various videos of Bosnian Muslim men who subsequently disappeared, but who have been identified. Copies of this -- and identified as missing and some that haven't been ever identified or located, or some that survived. Copies of this have been distributed, I think, pretty much at the same time as the other video stills book that we just discussed. As I understand it, there's no objection from my friends. This also eliminated the necessity to have an investigator, Ms. Gallagher, testify as to the creation of this document. And we would offer that as 1938. It's uploaded in e-court already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any remarks, objections, from any of the Defence teams? We hear none, so 1938 is admitted. More?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: One last item that I'm aware of, and that is the -- what we have been referring to as the duty officer notebook, volumes 1 and 2; that is, 65 ter 377. 377, Mr. President, I believe is the first volume --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I don't know why you are raising 377, because that formed part of the Butler list yesterday. It was not one of the documents that were objected to, and we have already admitted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Then I stand corrected, and nothing further to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the sequel to it is that there were bits and pieces of that document, of 377, that became other documents that were used with several other witnesses, and as a result of that, as a result of 377 being admitted yesterday, all the others have automatically been admitted. I can give you the details of those, if you want, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll pass. Thank you, Mr. President. And we do have a full translation of that document, as well as the other volume, and I've notified Mr. Haynes, in particular, some time ago about the completion of that project.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If the position is that the original P377, which is not the whole of the first Zvornik Brigade duty operations officer's notebook but merely a portion of it from, I think, about the 8th to the 20th of July - I might be wrong about those dates - has gone in as P377, together with odd bits and bobs, then that, in my submission, is a wholly unsatisfactory position, and what ought to be done is the translation of the whole book should supplant it as P377, rather than have one portion of the book and lots of little bits and bobs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you are in agreement -- if Mr. Thayer is in agreement to that, we can stop the discussion here and proceed accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, and I thank Mr. Thayer for his tireless efforts to get both of these volumes translated in what was a very short period of time. It's a difficult book to translate because it's all in manuscript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Thayer. Do you agree with Mr. Haynes' submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President. We do have full translations of both volumes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So what I propose to do is what we have always done. We don't prefer substitution of one with another. We would rather have what we have used so far, and we keep it 377, and the one which would, for all intents and purposes, be considered the one that you will be referring to as 377A or B or whatever number you find for it. The reason for this is that as was hinted at earlier on, witnesses may have already made reference to 377, particularly to particular pages, and so for reference purposes we better keep it there. And then of course we will use the entire one for the rest of the exercise, if that is agreeable to all of you. Okay. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Thayer. Yes. So you will follow this in due course and liaise with Mr. or Madam Registrar, as the case may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We will, Mr. President, and we also have -- just back to the video stills book, we have copies for the Chamber in production, and we'll deliver those when they're ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I'm addressing you not because I want to single you out, but because you have spoken on the matter already, and Mr. McCloskey. It's break time, but if you tell us that in relation to the pending motion on the documents to be offered from the Bar table, that there is an agreement that there will be no submissions today but that you will take your time to -- then our proposal, our suggestion, was if the rest of the staff agrees, that we proceed. I don't think we have got much more on the agenda today, unless we are missing something that we don't know, and finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I can speak on behalf of all my learned friends who are defending. Your Honour, the motion has now been filed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, but we haven't seen it as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Nor have we, but I can see it has now been filed. Realistically, we are not going to be in a position to address it today. I am thinking out loud, let me emphasise whether the Chamber needs to give some direction as to the respond, and in particular that -- well, they presumably will have no bearing on the 98 bis ruling. The documents aren't in evidence at the moment. The 98 bis is due to take place -- begin in a week's time, and I suspect most of us would want our 14 days to respond. I emphasise I'm thinking aloud. If any of my colleagues disagree, then no doubt they'll say, but that's what I'd ask for, our full 14 days to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's hear Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The Bar table motion has 46 documents total. Forty-four of those documents were in our intercept support motion and had already been determined by the Court to be relevant and probative on 11 January. So this isn't a real big deal, and I -- once counsel's had a chance to see the documents, they may or may not agree with me, but I don't think it's something that we need to spend court time to argue over. I'm willing to do it, of course, but that's -- it's not that big a deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to answer the question that you put. I'm not minded to make a submission about that motion today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you haven't even had time to put it in your mouth, let alone digest it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We haven't even been able to find some of the documents, as yet, but that may be our failing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully support my colleague Mr. Haynes. I believe that this motion is being filed much too late and does very much prejudice the Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nikolic -- Ms. Nikolic, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I wholly endorse what my colleagues have submitted, not to repeat what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I join that motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meek. You didn't address the question as to whether you would be able to live with the suggestion of Mr. Josse, that they will -- pending the determination of -- pending the resolution of this issue, that they will not form part of the documents to be taken into account for the purpose of Rule 98 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no problem with that. This doesn't need to interfere with the 98 bis process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All these documents have 65 ter numbers. As I say, I don't think it will amount -- this could be dealt with by paper, as far as I'm concerned. And as I say, that these are documents everyone's been on notice. We've litigated over all of them but two, so this isn't a situation where prejudice is involved in any way, shape, or form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That being said, do we have the go-ahead to sit for another maybe five, ten minutes, unless you have other things you would like to raise? We have got just two matters that we would like to dispose of, and then we can adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I've got about a minute or a minute and a half, but that's about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A minute is not going to change anything. Now ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we have now been formally informed that there is an urgent motion or a motion from -- not an urgent motion, a motion by the Prosecution, from the Prosecution, to seek admission of a number of documents from the Bar tables, as the saying goes. Our decision is that we will give this motion the chance to take its normal course. You will have the time limit set by the Rules to file your respective or joint responses, a consequence being that for the purpose of Rule 98 bis, these documents do not exist. Okay, that's number 1. Now, hope springs eternal, and yesterday -- also because we are optimistic by nature, the four of us. We sincerely believed that we could cut down -- shorten the time limit for Mr. McCloskey to respond to the Butler motion, and we also gave an indication that today we'd make an announcement on the Rupert Smith matter. It turned out to be somewhat more laborious and more complicated than we first thought. We have been actively discussing and discussing. I think we would be misleading you if we kept our promise and make you hope for a decision before you start with the Rule 98 bis submissions. We are sorry, but, I mean, we had expected the sittings to finish last week. We got one thing over the other, more witnesses, more sittings and more motions, and we found ourselves in a position today we realise we will not be able to make it. So bottom line is that for the purpose of Rule 98 bis, you would have to live with the consequence of our decision not to decide these two motions in time before the 14th of this month, and therefore, for all intents and purposes, you need to take into account, for the purposes of your submissions, the entirety of the testimony and reports of both Mr. Smith and Mr. -- General Smith and Mr. Butler. So that is the position. We have tried, but there are limits. One moment. I need to discuss something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We do not have any further matters to raise. If you have, please, let's do that as shortly as possible. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just a couple of things. You have accepted Mr. Butler's command reports into evidence. I think I mentioned, we do have CDs of those command reports where you can, when reading them, click on the cite and the document supporting comes up. That can't be done in e-court. We have those CDs, if the Court's interested. They also include the narratives, which are not in evidence yet, but of course you can ignore those. I also, I think as I mentioned, I have large copies of those smaller maps, if anyone wants them. I also -- there are two exhibits, two aerial images, 3009, which is an aerial image of the Branjevo Farm, which I briefly mentioned yesterday; and 1801, which is the Branjevo Farm on 27 September 1995, both of which have been the subject of some discussion in this case. I have what are hard copies of those photographs which are clearer than the electronic versions that are in e-court. I would like to provide those hard copies to the Court so that you have them to review, should you wish to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you provided them to the Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, for many months now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The first time I saw these aerial images was during my cross-examination of Dean Manning just before Christmas, so if that's "many months," then so be it. They're very significant. You might remember my cross-examination of Dean Manning about what the aerial images of Branjevo Farm apparently showed. I asked him to look at them and see whether he could compare certain things on photographs taken apparently on the 17th, the 21st and, I think, the 27th of July of 1995. During a break, a photograph was retrieved from the offices of the Office of the Prosecutor and was shown to me, and it seemed to me to be a very significant photograph indeed for one purpose for the Prosecution, but actually for a very good purpose for the Defence. It seemed to me to advance a point that Mr. Ostojic has been making forcefully throughout this trial about how certain things written in white boxes appeared on these photographs, because it compared directly to one that was then in evidence, but it had rather less writing on it. And when I pointed this out to Mr. McCloskey, the Prosecution took the tactical decision with Dean Manning, in re-examination, not to use this aerial image, doubtless aware of the fact that I might have applied for leave to re-cross-examine him to highlight the point that Mr. Ostojic has been trying to make for all these months. It seems to me it would be completely wrong, the Prosecution having decided not to put this photograph in through a witness several months ago, to borrow their phrase, to produce it from the Bar table now, so I do object. If there is a sensible course to this, it would be that they add a supplement to their current motion, and I will put these points in writing. When I asked Mr. McCloskey about this today, his explanation for not producing it through Dean Manning was that it was too late in the day. Well, today is even later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Do you wish to comment, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Had I offered to put that document in, having given them one hour's notice, the cry would have been heard around the world of prejudice, and that is why I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, it wouldn't. I was ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: They're tougher in England, but there would have been other objections, and that's why I gave them plenty of time to digest it. This issue has been churned and churned by Mr. Ostojic. So these documents are fundamentally already in evidence. The versions of these things, the electronic version that they've had for a while, is very similar to the hard-copy versions. These hard-copy versions are a little clearer. In my view, you can clearly see the back-loader -- the backhoe and loader in them, and I think you'll agree with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not go into the details. Leave it as a procedural matter. I think if you give me a moment to consult with my colleagues ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, sorry to cut you short and in an abrupt manner, but it will also dispose of the matter. We have discussed it. We're on the same wavelength while you were both contributing to the discussion, to the debate. The situation being what it is, in other words, the diametrically-opposed positions that you have taken, for the moment we don't need these documents, we don't want them. If they are made use of later on in the day during this trial, we may reconsider our position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One other request. I think I may have made this before, but as we are approaching the 98 bis stage, any particular areas that you would like us to focus on would, of course, be appreciated. Of course, we also appreciate being left in the dark, and that's not a problem. But if there are any particular areas, we will be ready to respond to those. And I would also ask my colleagues, as I'm sure none of them will, but anyone that is planning waiving 98 bis, the sooner we know that, that would also be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, don't rush. I don't think we have anything to tell you. You are all aware of what Rule 98 bis is all about. It's a motion to acquit. Admittedly, it could also be triggered ex officio, but it is basically a motion to acquit. The standards have been set by our case law, and I don't think we need to elaborate on that. You need to stick to what is required by the Rule and by the jurisprudence, and not treat the procedure as if we have come to the end of the case and discuss the merits and ultimate acquittal. So I think it's clear enough, and we are confident that you understand exactly what the whole procedure is all about, while it's still there in our Rules. All right. And, of course, Defence go first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In that event, Mr. President, I think the Prosecution can rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we've come to the end of the first leg of a long journey. Before we adjourn until Thursday of next week for the first submissions, Rule 98 bis submissions, I wish to thank you for all the work that you have put during the past months in the case, in the interests of your respective case, in the case of the Prosecution, and in your case in the interest of your clients; but also in the interests of justice. So the first hurdle is over, we now need to overcome the second one, the Rule 98 bis decision; and then we embark on the next leg, which will also be a long one and as complicated as the one we have just finished. So I wish you all a nice evening and a nice weekend, and I'm sure you are not going to enjoy yourself this weekend and that you will be engaged in preparing for your contributions next week. Thank you. And one moment. I also wish to thank, as usual, the staff. You're always so prepared and so forthcoming to help the Tribunal in trying to economize on time. I don't know how to show my appreciation, except to communicate it formally to the Registrar and to your immediate superiors. Infallibly during these months, you've been extremely, extremely cooperative. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 14th day of February, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.08 p.m.,
